Why APL feedback makes the effect of blocking uneven across odors

QuestionWhy does blocking a uniform, feedback APL raise the similarity of some odor pairs more than others, and do the recordings show the same signature?

Report 07 found that a uniform APL with feedback predicts which pairs gain similarity when APL is blocked about as well as any wiring version. This report explains why, in two steps. First, feedback makes the inhibition odor-dependent, so blocking it adds the most responders to strong odors. Second, an odor that gains responders becomes more similar to every other odor by chance overlap alone.

What changed in this revision (2026-11-04)

The four inhibition rules as a table: only feedback is a model; the other three are reference rules.

New: how the Spearman values are computed, with -aPine as a worked example.

γo\gamma_oγo​ is now called the "blocked ÷ intact ratio", so it is not confused with the input gain gog_ogo​ of Report 07.

In the ratio figure the data are drawn as open diamonds, so model points at the same place stay visible.

Odor strength in the data is now measured in TNT only, with the earlier mean of TNT and TNT3c kept for comparison.

Numbers come from the run with the corrected calyx, the new claws and the new ORN table.

1Step 1: feedback inhibits strong odors more

With a uniform APL, every KC gets the same inhibition aAoa A_oaAo​ for odor ooo (Report 05). It is the same for every KC, but not for every odor: AoA_oAo​ is the mean KC response, so an odor that drives many KCs recruits a lot of APL and is held down hard, and one that drives few recruits little. Feedback therefore evens out how many KCs the odors activate, like a normalization, and blocking APL undoes it. To show that feedback is what matters, three other rules for the inhibition are compared. All four start from the same pinned, blocked responses ykoblocked=[xko−1]+y^{\mathrm{blocked}}_{ko} = [x_{ko} - 1]_+ykoblocked​=[xko​−1]+​ and give the same mean fraction responding over odors (TNT3c's, 6.83%). They differ only in how the inhibition is shared out between odors (Table 2).

The three extra rules are not new models of APL. They are controls that keep everything the same except how the inhibition depends on the odor: not at all (fixed), in proportion to the odor's own blocked response (same share), or exactly as in the data (TNT3c per odor). Comparing feedback with them shows whether the odor-dependence created by feedback is what matters for the fit.

With feedback, the blocked ÷ intact ratio rises with odor strength (Spearman +0.92 over odors), from ×1.68 to ×2.56. A fixed raise does the opposite (Spearman -0.55): weak odors lose the largest share of their few responders, because a fixed raise removes a fixed slice of the drive distribution near threshold. In the data the ratio is barely related to the TNT fraction (Spearman +0.22).

1.1How the Spearman values are computed: -aPine as an example

For each of the 16 odors there are two numbers, each the mean over the three mushroom bodies: the fraction responding with APL blocked (ϕoblocked\phi^{\mathrm{blocked}}_oϕoblocked​, equal to the TNT fraction by pinning) and the ratio γo=ϕoblocked/ϕointact\gamma_o = \phi^{\mathrm{blocked}}_o / \phi^{\mathrm{intact}}_oγo​=ϕoblocked​/ϕointact​. The Spearman correlation is the Pearson correlation of their ranks over the 16 odors.

For -aPine, ϕblocked\phi^{\mathrm{blocked}}ϕblocked = 6.07% and ϕintact\phi^{\mathrm{intact}}ϕintact with feedback = 3.61%, so γ\gammaγ = 6.07 / 3.61 = 1.68 (rank 1 of 16 by ratio, rank 1 of 16 by blocked fraction). The data's value is 6.05 / 3.57 = 1.70. This γo\gamma_oγo​ is not the input gain gog_ogo​ of Report 07, which for -aPine is large because its ORN responses are weak.

2Step 2: from more responders to more similarity

Denser codes overlap more by chance. For 0/1 responses the cosine similarity is the overlap divided by the geometric mean of the code sizes:

cos⁡(a,b)=nabna nb(1)\cos(a, b) = \frac{n_{ab}}{\sqrt{n_a\, n_b}} \tag{1}cos(a,b)=na​nb​​nab​​(1)

If odor bbb's responders are placed at random, independently of aaa's, the overlap nabn_{ab}nab​ follows a hypergeometric distribution with mean nanb/Nn_a n_b / Nna​nb​/N. The expected cosine is therefore

E[cos⁡(a,b)]=nanb/Nnanb=pa pb,SD≈(1−pa)(1−pb)N−1(2)\mathbb{E}[\cos(a, b)] = \frac{n_a n_b / N}{\sqrt{n_a n_b}} = \sqrt{p_a\, p_b}, \qquad \mathrm{SD} \approx \sqrt{\frac{(1-p_a)(1-p_b)}{N-1}} \tag{2}E[cos(a,b)]=na​nb​​na​nb​/N​=pa​pb​​,SD≈N−1(1−pa​)(1−pb​)​​(2)

So an odor that gains responders becomes more similar to every other odor, and its whole row of the similarity matrix rises. This is the link between Step 1 (per-odor gains) and the per-odor part of ΔS\Delta SΔS (Report 06, Section 4).

A floor, not the exact chance level, for KCs

The formula assumes every unit is equally likely to respond. If unit kkk responds with probability πk\pi_kπk​, the expected cosine is about (papb+covk(πa,πb))/papb(p_a p_b + \mathrm{cov}_k(\pi_{a}, \pi_{b}))/\sqrt{p_a p_b}(pa​pb​+covk​(πa​,πb​))/pa​pb​​, which is higher when the same units respond easily to both odors. In the connectome model, two unrelated odors that each drive 10% of KCs have a cosine of 1.54 × papb\sqrt{p_a p_b}pa​pb​​ with the ORN-table glomeruli, and 1.17 × with every glomerulus responding, because some KCs are easier to drive than others.

In the data the real 0/1 similarity is about twice papb\sqrt{p_a p_b}pa​pb​​ in both conditions (0.145 vs 0.066 in TNT3c, 0.289 vs 0.144 in TNT). That excess can come from related odors or from units that respond to many odors. A shuffle that keeps each unit's number of responses and each odor's fraction reproduces the mean (0.145 in TNT3c), so with 16 odors the two cannot be told apart.

3Step 3: which inhibition rule fits the data

  • Feedback fits better than a fixed raise in every mushroom body and in 100% of bootstrap draws (r 0.49 vs 0.37 with ORN input).
  • Feedback does as well as setting each odor's intact fraction from the data (r 0.49), although it is not given the per-odor TNT3c fractions.
  • The per-odor part of the change matches the data with Spearman 0.62 for feedback and 0.37 for a fixed raise.

4Step 4: is the feedback signature in the recordings?

If APL acted as uniform feedback, odors that drive more units should gain more units when APL is blocked. Odor strength is measured in TNT, where APL is blocked: there it reflects the feed-forward drive from the PNs, and it is what the model's horizontal axis in Figure 1 uses. TNT3c is already evened out by feedback, so mixing it in would blur the measure. To avoid shared noise, strength and ratio come from separate halves of the recordings: 4 TNT recordings give the strength, and the other 4 TNT and 6 of the 11 TNT3c recordings give the ratio. This is repeated for 2,000 random splits.

  • Units responding: the ratio is weakly related to odor strength (mean split-half Spearman +0.13, 5–95% −0.13 to +0.41, positive in 79% of splits), far from the +0.92 that uniform feedback predicts. The spread across odors is about the same in TNT and TNT3c (CV 0.32 and 0.31), whereas uniform feedback predicts less spread with APL intact.
  • Response size: stronger odors do gain more (Spearman +0.34 for the mean positive response, positive in 99.5% of splits).
  • Measuring strength from the mean of TNT and TNT3c, as in the earlier version, gives the same conclusion (Table 3).
  • So the recordings show the feedback signature in response size but only weakly, if at all, in the number of responding units.
Caveats

The rules other than feedback are not mechanisms; they are reference points with the same mean inhibition.

Noise inflates TNT3c's apparent number of weak responders differently from TNT's, which can blur the gain-vs-strength relation.
